text.content: Sometimes the street respects style over substance. Wave a big gun in someone’s face and they usually won’t care whether it’s jam-prone—or even loaded. On the other hand, you need gear that works. Someday they’ll call your bluff, and all that chrome-plated bluster won’t save you from explosive rounds designed to down cyborgs. But occasionally, style is substance. In a world where networks record every move, algorithms push ads for everything from body armor to print-on-demand snacks, and implants provide posthuman abilities, the technology you use becomes part of your personal identity. As you peruse this chapter, consider these factors. Note, however, that the items don’t include posthuman body alterations, which can be found in Chapter 3.

It practically goes without saying that technology is central to the cyberpunk genre, though not necessarily due to speculation about the future. While that element isn’t entirely absent, cyberpunk fiction often uses technology to highlight contemporary social, political, and psychological themes as well. One common element, as mentioned above, is that the tech you use not only says something about who you are but influences your identity. As you adopt new technologies, they change your behavior. Sometimes this opens amazing opportunities for work and play. Sometimes it leads to chaos, poverty, and dystopian outcomes. The cyberpunk genre has both tendencies.

Social & Personal Change

This book was written in 2021, during the COVID-19, pandemic, amidst an unprecedented migration to working from home which may outlast its origins. Now combine that with highly mobile, dexterous robots, and even front-line industrial and retail work become work from home positions, assuming humans are required to teleoperate robots (that is, control them through remote connections) for complex tasks. If not, automation causes enormous social changes as an enormous pool of labor finds their skills are no longer required. Either way, the situation creates a new kind of society.

If teleoperation does become routine, however, that means more than being able to work “in-person” from a home office. As a robot operator, you effectively have a second body. You might develop a distinct personality while working through a robot, with its own name and voice. You might even customize your robot—or suffer from forced anonymity if a corporation forbids it. If we upgrade from the kind of teleoperation possible today to a direct mind-machine connection, your life as a robot could include being truly embodied as one, with a full suite of human-like—or better—senses. And what if these robots were available to consumers? How often might you live in another body? What experiences are possible now that human flesh could never withstand?

This is just one example of using technology to shape your character, and even a campaign itself. Some cyberpunk fiction focuses just on one or two transformational technologies,

In cyberpunk fiction characters often encounter technology superior even to the world’s heightened baseline. For minor technological superiority, add the following quality to an item.

Advanced

When using this item for the purpose it was designed for, you gain +1 stunt point from rolling doubles.

Use this when something is advanced relative to the general sophistication of technology in the campaign. If most other technologies attain the same level, remove the quality.

while other inspirations take a full spectrum “future shock” approach, where numerous new technologies create a strange future built upon intelligible foundations.

Brand Recognition

Like we said before, style matters, and a part of that is brand recognition: the notion that certain things are just inherently cooler and more stylish because of who makes them, what they’re called, or the logo emblazoned on them. While the equipment details in this chapter are generic and focused on their benefits in game terms, players and Game Masters are encouraged to enhance them with suitable brand-names and stylish descriptions. What sounds more kick-ass: A “subma-chine gun” or an “H&K MP-10 Alpha with folding stock”? A suit of “armored cloth” or “Widow-X spider-silk street wear”? Feel free to come up with cool brands, looks, and styles for the various equipment discussed in this chapter, even if their game mechanics are the same as usual.

Sometimes, however, you’ll want some brands to pack an extra punch. Maybe they live up to the hype! Modern AGE uses the reputation rules (Modern AGE Basic Rulebook, pp. 154-157) to recognize how others see you, based on your actual and purported accomplishments. This element shows up in cyberpunk fiction as well, but for corporate entities and brands as well as people. Therefore, we recommend you adapt the reputation rules for better-regarded brands.

In game terms, this means characters can purchase (or otherwise acquire) branded gear that possesses reputation honorifics. A brand is developed a little differently from personal reputation, however. Most of the tech belonging to a single brand has a common honorific, so instead of devising honorifics by item or owner, you set in by brand. Consequently, this means you can develop brands and honorifics to flesh out your campaign setting. See the Sample Brands sidebar for details.

You can only benefit from one brand at a time. However, you can stack a brand with your personal reputation honorific, and any negative effects for passive reputation remain for all the brands you have on display.

Good and Bad Brands

Brands with reputation features have something in common: They’re attached to respected consumer goods. There are plenty of brands known for being ugly, breaking down, and so on, but these don’t use reputation rules. The GM should attach disadvantages to these items and note their brands. Characters will eventually recognize which brands have good reputations and which ones don’t.

Brands Cost Money

Brands with reputation features cost more than generic versions of the same items. This usually increases their Resources cost by 2, though luxury brands may add 3 or more to the listed base cost of goods. Quality brands are in high demand as well, so a character flaunting their branded gear might get mugged for it. This becomes especially dangerous for characters with branded augmentations.

Branded Augmentations

Cyberware and other augmentations from Chapter 3 can also be branded. If the Game Master makes characters pay for branded augmentation, the Resources modifications from Brands Cost Money apply. If not, the brand forces a Resources test with a TN of 13 + the TN modification that would apply if the augmentation was a conventional item.

Automation

AI, machine learning, data processing at scale, and a host of related advancements lead to routine automation. In this book, we reflect that with Automation Classes representing various degrees of sophistication. These degrees are listed in the Automation Classes table and explained further in this section. These rules assume largely assume a Pulpy or Cinematic Mode. See Gritty Automation for a discussion of the “realistic” options. Here and there, we refer to devices benefiting from automation as automata (singular: automaton).

Automation Class

This rates how sophisticated a device’s automation systems are. This also includes its ability to adapt to new and unusual situations. It takes true intelligence, or at least extremely sophisticated programming, to act as flexibly as a human. All automata can perform the tasks inherent to their designed within precisely defined instructions, which are typically reduced to keyword shortcuts such as “Take me to Boston,” or, “Sentry mode on.” The GM ultimately decides how smart they are, but as a guide, use the descriptions below.

Poor

The cheapest automated devices, as well as those hacked together from a few circuit boards and slapdash code, belong to this class. They’re typically unreliable and can’t perform unusual actions by themselves. A Poor automaton may do strange and even self-destructive things by following its programming regardless of the changing situation. A Poor

The following brands serve as examples or starting points for brands in your own campaign.

Appsoft

Appsoft’s an omnipresent brand, appearing on the UIs and etched into the magnesium-polymer composite bodies of numerous devices. Appsoft products were originally favored by VR designers and other creative information professionals, but for decades they’ve been treated as a slightly posh consumer brand.

Industry: Computer hardware and software.

Honorific: The reliable but feature-bloated high end consumer standard.

Asher-Tesser Realities

This privately held Anglo-German corporation was created through that most antique of institutions, political marriage. It remains a virtual fiefdom of the media-averse Asher-Tesser family, who direct funding to AI and VR research in what may be anything from a bid for cybernetic immortality to a moonshot gaming project. It makes its money selling the byproducts of this mysterious project to an assortment of corporate and government clients, though its human-computer interface devices have some traction among well-heeled consumers.

Industry: Machine intelligence and virtual reality.

Honorific: Strange and innovative, with unexpected features.

D|Z

D|Z was once Drop/Zone, but that manifestation of the brand lasted about a year, though the name remains on legal documents and DZ user guides. D|Z | gear isn’t especially high quality, but it’s not bad, and it always looks good.

Basic

The class possessed by devices in most controlled environments. Security drones following set routes and factory-floor robots have Basic automation. A Basic device can occasionally adapt to unusual situations, but only to perform its core func-

They’re the premiere brand for personal technology as street fashion.

Industry: Audiovisual and VR gear fashion brand.

Honorific: Mandatory style minimum if you want to avoid off-brand hell.

Longquan Sword Military Industries

For centuries, the city of Longquan, China has been known for metalwork, especially in the form of sword making. LSMI adds advanced small arms technology and cybernetics to the mix, with an emphasis on reliable, simple design even in the modest advanced weapon implants. It’s easy to get off-brand duplicates of their basic designs, but true LSMI quality is hard to buy unless you’re a vetted military or security client.

Industry: Small arms and close combat weaponry, carried or implanted.

Honorific: Tough, reliable, and straightforward mil-tech.

Penumbrè

Penumbrè is the modern incarnation of the Belgian design house founded by Pierre Hermans in 1829. After Belgium’s colonial wealth declined, successors moved Pierre Hermans Design to Paris, where its handbags and other fashion accessories became icons of European style. The company rebranded in 1968 to avoid colonial associations, and while it’s still viewed as a problematic brand, it remains one of the most prestigious fashion brands in the world, with prices to match— Penumbrè-branded goods cost +4 Resources more than typical counterparts.

Industry: Luxury goods such as bags, scents, clothing, personal electronics, and fashion augmentations.

Honorific: Wearing Penumbrè is aristocrat-level luxury, elite and problematic.

Advanced

The highest degree of consumer-grade automation. Advanced-class devices can incorporate natural-language orders into autonomous reactions. You can give the automaton “marching orders” outside its direct functions (such as “Shoot the next person to talk about Indra Winchester,” as opposed to shooting any non-friendly in a certain radius or anyone who doesn’t use a passcode) and it will be smart enough to follow them. It isn’t smart enough to resolve contradictory or excessively vague instructions (if the GM doesn’t understand what you want, that qualifies), and may run into problems if given them.

Restricted

Devised for classified military and intelligence operations, Restricted-class automation devises new reactions based on algorithms simulating instinct. A Restricted automaton functions as best it can in any environment according to a top-level core mission. It can assign variable priorities to different actions, including user commands, based on the core mission and the behavior patterns of users.

Secret

This degree of automation is usually possessed by conscious AIs. Secret-rated devices react with at least the intelligence of a human expert in its functions, in all conditions where it is capable of operating.

Test Bonus

The modifier to tests granted by the listed automation class, replacing the ability + focus modifier of a human (or human-equivalent) operator. This applies to anything the automaton can do. Individual devices may have further modifiers to specific actions. If a separate ability rating is required, calculate it as the bonus -2.

Automated tests can gain and use stunt points but are limited by their class in that they cannot use SP to perform an action outside the range of tasks they can perform. For example, a gun with Basic automation can spend SP on Brutal Blow and Lightning Attack, as these fit its default functions, but can’t use Skirmish to move opponents for the sake of a tactical advantage.

By strictly realistic but speculative standards, the automation rules here are underpowered. Automated systems are already superior to humans in accuracy and reaction time and have grown increasingly context sensitive. However, this leads to things like vehicles which perform high speed maneuvers flawlessly, and perhaps more gravely, automated weapons that never miss. Therefore, we recommend you use the non-Gritty default option, even in Gritty games. If you want more realistic automation, consider the following options:

Hardcore Gritty Automation

Automata automatically succeed at all tests their systems can execute as if they had rolled an 18 on 3d6, and a degree of success of 5 + the device’s Aid Bonus, but they never gain stunt points. That, at least, is available to flawed humans and their synthetic cousins. This isn’t recommended, but it’s there if you want it.

Pretty Gritty Automation

Add +3 to all Routine Actions and allow them to be used for attack rolls, which is normally disallowed. This gives an aura of extreme effectiveness to automata without pushing them over the edge, and favors Routine Actions, which do not benefit from stunt points.

Jamming Everywhere

If you use this option, Hardcore or Pretty Gritty automation is the default, but devices almost always make exceptions for Player Characters. This is because PCs are assumed to have counter-automation systems that affect devices whenever they might potentially harm or otherwise disadvantage them, reducing their functionality to the default Pulpy/Cinematic style in this section. Likewise, all NPCs have similar systems. These might be tough chunks of portable hardware consisting of a transmitter and a virus-breeding algorithm, a network-distributed service, a hack spread through omnipresent nanorobots, or whatever else leads to automata being theoretically more powerful, but practically limited.

Aid Bonus

When a human or other third-party operator uses the device, the listed degree of automation provides this bonus to tests, limited to tasks defined by the automaton’s class.

Routine Action

Optionally, an automated device can replace a dice roll with a routine action. This automatically scores the listed number instead of a roll result, as modified by any conditions the GM feels appropriate. The number in parenthesis is the degree of success, if required. This makes automata reliable, but routine actions come with a drawback: They cannot gain or use stunt points. In Pulpy and Cinematic Modes, this option is unusable with attack rolls or by devices with Poor-class automation.

Weapons

You can use the basic selection of weapons from the Modern AGE Basic Rulebook as a starting point for a cyberpunk setting, which offers some enhanced versions of existing weapons, along with a few new weapons options. The basic technology of most weapons remains unchanged, with refinements and enhancements to the implementation.

In general, cyberpunk weapons tend to make use of advanced composites, ceramics, polycarbonate, and similar materials along with improved manufacturing techniques. Things like 3-D printing, combined with the right materials, may even put otherwise restricted weapons onto the streets and into the hands of anyone able to make and assemble the parts. Certainly, there is likely to be a brisk black-market in illegal weapons of all kinds.

Futuristic Weapons

Game Masters may want to reflect improvements in weapon design and construction in a cyberpunk setting. Consider adding one of the following qualities to existing Modern AGE weapons. These are different from the advanced quality, as they represent improvements to the technological baseline, while advanced items are superior to the baseline, even in a cyberpunk future.

Effective

The weapon does its job better, inflicting +1 damage.

Light

The weapon is exceptionally light, reducing its minimum Strength by 1.

High Capacity

Caseless ammunition, or smaller rounds that pack a greater punch, increase your weapon’s Capacity by 1. If this leads to a Capacity higher than 6, it stays at 6, but you may ignore one reload prompt per encounter.

Tough

This weapon is made of strong materials. Stunts that would normally destroy it have no effect, and if directly attacked, it has an Armor Rating 2I/2B higher than normal.

Weapon Details

Along with the weapons detailed in the Modern AGE Basic Rulebook, the following weapons are common in cyberpunk settings.

Unarmed

Knuckle Spikes: Heavy bands worn over the knuckles, usually equipped with spikes or ridges to inflict +1 additional damage to the wearer’s unarmed brawling strikes.

Shock Knuckles: Compact battery packs with conductive surfaces over the wearer’s knuckles, shock knuckles inflict a potent electrical shock when they strike a target, much like a stun baton: The target must succeed on a Constitution (Stamina) test with a TN of 10 + damage inflicted by the brawling strike or be paralyzed for 1d6 rounds. If the brawling strike does not inflict any damage due to the target’s armor, no test against the paralyzing effect is needed.

Short Hafted Weapons

Collapsible Baton: A telescoping rod of metal or carbon-fiber that extends from pocket-sized and easily concealable to the equivalent of a club usable in hand-to-hand combat.

Light and Heavy Blades

Monofilament Blade: Cyberpunk blades may be equipped with a monofilament edge, honed incredibly sharp. This adds +2 to the weapon’s normal damage and the wielder of a monofilament blade can perform the Precise Force stunt for 1 SP rather than 2. If they choose to spend 2 SP on the stunt, it ignores all the target’s Armor Rating from equipment.

Flexible Weapons

Monofilament Whip: A strand of monofilament extending up the three meters, with a small weight at the end to control its swing and a handle the filament can retract into when not in use. A monofilament whip (or simply “mono-whip”) is a nearly invisible, razor-sharp flexible weapon. Its wielder can perform the Precise Force stunt for 1 SP rather than 2 and, if they choose to spend 2 SP on the stunt, ignore all the target’s armor rating from equipment. The wielder can also perform the Lightning Attack stunt for 1 SP rather than 2 and can perform the stunt multiple times, until one of the attacks misses. Wielding a mono-whip is dangerous, however. Firearms

Cyberpunk-era firearms often feature caseless ammunition and may be constructed from polycarbonate or ceramic compounds to fool metal-detectors. 3D printing may make the creation of firearm parts and their construction available to almost anyone, assuming gun access and ownership isn’t simply universal in the setting.

The various types of firearms found in the Modern AGE Basic Rulebook serve for the kinds of weapons available to cyberpunk characters, with the differences of manufacturing and branding mentioned previously, and the additions of different ammunition types and firearms accessories following (see Ammunition and Firearms Accessories).

Thrown Weapons

Shuriken: Various types of Japanese “throwing stars” (or throwing spikes for bo shuriken) are forms of throwing knives that often appear in cyberpunk settings. They use the same stats as throwing knives from the Modern AGE Basic Rulebook.

Grenades

Grenades in cyberpunk settings tend to be smaller and more compact, often not much bigger than large ball-bearings. Some types of grenades, particularly blast grenades, may also come in the form of flat discs with a magnetic clamp on one

This allows them to be slapped onto the sides of vehicles, some structures, and sometimes even individual targets containing or wearing enough metal, such as heavily augmented opponents. The grenade’s fuse can be pre-set to go off in 1–5 rounds after activation. Removing a magnetically clamped grenade requires a TN 17 Strength (Might) test.

The following additional types of grenades are common in cyberpunk settings.

Flash-Bangs: A flash-bang emits a loud noise and a bright flash of light, intended to blind, deafen, and stun targets. Anyone within 5 yards of the grenade when it goes off must make a TN 15 Constitution (Stamina) test. If it fails, they lose their next round of actions, and are at a –2 penalty on all tests for 1d6 rounds thereafter. If the test succeeds, the target is at only a –1 penalty for 1d3 rounds.

Smoke: This grenade releases a cloud of thick, white smoke intended to provide cover. The cloud is 5 yards in radius and provides a –3 penalty to ranged attack tests and Perception (Seeing) tests against anything inside the area or crossing the cloud’s boundary. It lasts for 3 + 1d6 rounds before dissipating, although it may clear faster if there is a strong wind or the like.

Tear Gas: A tear gas grenade is like a smoke grenade (previously) but also has a chemical irritant that burns the eyes and lungs. The grenade releases a cloud of gas 5 yards in radius, lasting for 3 + 1d6 rounds. When a target enters the cloud of tear gas, or begins their turn there, they must roll a TN 15 Constitution (Tolerance) test. On a failure, they may only take a single major or minor action on their turn (not both) and are at a –2 penalty to all tests. If the Constitution (Tolerance) test succeeds, the target is at only a –1 penalty to all tests. The effects of the tear gas last for 2d6 rounds after the character leaves the cloud’s area or until the character successfully receives first aid, which ends the effect.

Ammunition

Often innovations in weapons technology for cyberpunk-era firearms are in terms of the ammunition a weapon fires (or the accessories added to it, following). These types of ammo may be available for firearms in a cyberpunk setting.

Armor Piercing: These bullets use special coatings and materials to make them more easily penetrate and slide through armor. Armor piercing rounds allow a character firing the weapon to use the Precise Force stunt with a ballistic damage weapon and for –1 SP cost, but the weapon also does 1 point less damage, due to the tendency of the rounds not to spread, but instead go cleanly through their target.

Dart: The weapon fires hypodermic darts, which can be loaded with various drugs. Sedatives are the most common. The darts themselves inflict only negligible damage, and 1 or more points of Impact armor blocks them (absent a called shot, see Hit Locations and Called Shots under Armor, following). Darts are not interchangeable with regular ammo and require weapons specifically designed to fire them. See DRUGS for possible dart round loads (not included in the cost of the darts).

Explosive: The opposite of armor piercing bullets in some ways, explosive bullets spread and flatted even more when they strike their target, causing more pronounced damage. Explosive bullets inflict +2 damage to “soft” targets with no

Ballistic armor, but –2 damage against targets that do have Ballistic armor.

Flechette: Rather than bullets, the firearm shoots small, sharp shards of metal or plastic, inflicting Impact rather than Ballistic damage. This makes Impact armor far more effective against a flechette weapon but Ballistic armor less effective. Flechette ammo is not interchangeable and requires a weapon specifically designed to fire it; flechette guns cannot fire regular bullets nor can regular guns fire flechette ammo.

Gel: These rounds are soft “gels” filled with liquid, designed to burst on impact, like paintball rounds, which just stain a target with a colored pigment. A gel round inflicts only 1 point of stun damage, easily overcome by armor and Toughness, but it is usually what the round carries that is a concern. In addition to paint, gel rounds might be loaded with skin irritants (requiring a Constitute (Tolerance) test to avoid a penalty to all tests due to distraction, typically TN 13 and a –2 penalty). They might also use a solution of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) as a carrier for certain drugs; the DMSO makes the drug absorbed through the skin, if hit by the gel rounds. See Drugs for possible gel loads (not included in the cost of the gel rounds).

Stun: “Stun” rounds are like gel rounds but designed for more impact. In truth, it causes the firearm to inflict half its usual damage as ballistic stun damage, and half as impact wound damage. Stun rounds can still be lethal; apply their impact wound damage first, and if that brings the target to 0 or less Health, they suffer the normal effects. If the stun damage brings them to 0 Health, they are merely left unconscious.

Taser: Like dart ammo (previously) except taser darts contain high-density batteries designed to deliver a powerful electric shock to the target. They function like the stun gun described in Chapter 4 of the Modern AGE Basic Rulebook, except they do not require the trailing wires, being self-contained, and have a greater range. Taser darts require a weapon specially designed to fire them and are not interchangeable with other types of ammo.

Tracer: Bullets trail a bright “tracer” line through the air, easily visible, particularly in darkness or dim light, showing their trajectory. Tracers are typically used in automatic weapons, with every third or fourth bullet a tracer round. Whenever a character performs an Automatic Weapon stunt using a gun loaded with tracers, they gain an additional +1 bonus to their next attack roll with that weapon as the tracers help them to aim.

Firearm Accessories

A variety of add-on accessories make firearms more effective in a cyberpunk setting. These accessories are often signs of professional mercenaries and assassins, who use the finest “tools of their trade.”

Biometric Lock: The weapon’s grip has sensors allowing it to read finger- and palm-prints, and it unlocks its safeties only for authorized users. This prevents a weapon from being taken and used against its owner. In some cyberpunk settings, a biometric lock might also be remote-controlled, such as in the case of a security or police force who can only use certain weapons with permission from their higher-ups at headquarters.

Flash Suppressor: A muzzle attachment suppresses the usual flash from expanding gases of a fired bullet, so only the sound of a gunshot gives away the firer’s position. It is often combined with a silencer (following) for stealth attacks using firearms.

Grenade Launcher: An under-barrel attachment for long-arms and rifles, a grenade launcher can load and fire grenades built for it, eliminating the need to throw them. This gives the grenade a range of 50 yards, and it is targeted using the Longarms or Shotguns focus rather than the Thrown focus. Reloading a grenade launcher is a minor action.

Laser Sight: A low-level laser attached to the gun’s barrel “paints” a small red dot of light where the gun is aimed. A laser light increases the bonus provided by the Aim action to +2. Futuristic laser sights can create dots in non-visible spectra, making them invisible to natural human eyes.

Silencer, Advanced: A muzzle attachment baffles the expanding gases from a gunshot better than a modern-day flash suppressor. In addition to having the sound effects of a suppressor (see p. 79 of Modern AGE) the advanced silencer changes the difficulty to hear the gunshot from automatic to a TN 9 Perception (Hearing) test. Advanced silencers are common accessories for assassins.

Smartgun: A smartgun has an on-board computer linked to the user, who must have a commlink implant (see the AUGMENTATIONS chapter for details). The gun transmits telemetry to its user, providing a floating “gunsight” in their line of vision that provides a +1 bonus to attack tests, which stacks with the +2 bonus for aiming with a laser sight (previously). The smartgun also provides data line range to the target, current ammo load, and the ability to designate “friendly” targets that lock-out the gun’s firing mechanism so it cannot accidentally shoot at them. A smartgun may even remove the weapon’s mechanical trigger entirely, fired solely by mental command by its wielder, although this also renders the gun inoperative if the smartgun link is inactive for any reason.

Armor

Armor is common in cyberpunk settings, given the proliferation of weapons and improvements in technology that make effective armor easy to wear and conceal. Advanced materials like polycarbonate monofilament and modified spider-silk derivatives, among others, can produce fabrics as light and flexible as ordinary cloth, but resistant to the impact of bullets and other weapons. The focus of cyberpunk armor tends to be protecting against ballistic damage, given the proliferation of guns, which in turn makes proficiency with archaic melee and throwing weapons an advantage for professional fighters and killers.

Hit Locations & Called Shots

Since armor rarely covers a target’s entire body, an attack’s location can matter in terms of the armor’s effectiveness. Generally, since most weapon hits tend to be in the torso area, the Game Master can just assume armor is effective against most attacks, applying the worn Armor Rating against all damage. In cases where it is important to know exactly where a target is hit, or if an attacker wishes to aim for a specific area (usually to avoid the target’s armor), you can use the following guidelines:

Take the lowest number showing on the dice for the attack roll and consult the Hit Locations table. For example, if an attack roll comes up 5, 3, and 3, you would reference the “3” line of the table, resulting in a hit on the target’s dominant arm.

The number after the slash for each location is the attack roll penalty to specifically target that area. If you take the penalty to your attack roll and it succeeds, you hit that location instead of using the lowest die from your attack roll to determine location. The attack’s damage is reduced by armor worn over that area, if any. Otherwise, hitting a specific area has no additional effects, although it might also justify spending SP on specific stunts.

Layered Armor

Some cyberpunk armor is light enough that it can be worn over or under other armor, such as wearing an armor jacket over armor clothing, for example. If a character layers armor in this way, the Armor Ratings are not additive. Instead, apply a +1 to bonus to the rating of the highest-rated armor per additional layer, so long as the lower-rated layers have ratings at least half that of the highest-rated layer. The layered armor uses the highest Armor Penalty among the layers (even if it is not the one with the highest armor rating) and increases that Armor Penalty by 1 per added layer, even if that layer normally has a penalty of 0.

The Game Master ultimately decides if it is reasonable to layer certain types of armor. Generally, two to three layers at most will be the effective limit, short of a character walking around like they are wearing an inflatable armored suit. At the GM’s discretion, layered armor may also be more noticeable, applying the armor’s Penalty as a bonus to Perception tests to notice the character is wearing armor, in addition to it reducing their Speed and Dexterity.

If a character wears armor clothing (2I/4B, 0 penalty) under an armor jacket (4I/6B, –1 penalty) the character has an armor rating of 5I/7B (the rating of the jacket +1) and an armor penalty of –2 (the penalty of the jacket, –1 more for the additional layer).

Armor Descriptions

The following types of armor are commonly available in cyberpunk settings.

Armor Clothing: Ordinary-looking clothing made from ballistic cloth and specially reinforced materials that offer some protection against bullets and other weapons.

Armor Vest: Light, close-fitting torso armor that can be worn underneath ordinary or armor clothing, offering an additional layer of protection.

Armor Jacket: The equivalent of a leather jacket, and often styled to look like one, but lined with ballistic cloth and reinforced with light armor plates to provide additional protection. A similar armored “duster” is a long coat like those worn in the American Old West that provides additional protection around the wearer’s legs.

Street Leathers: Modified biker leathers backed up by ballistic cloth linings for added protection. Often worn with a biker helmet of advanced ceramic composites with an opaque or mirrored faceplate suitable for use as a head-up display and an integral and voice-activated comm system.

Assault Armor: This is heavy security armor worn by elite rent-a-cops and police officers expecting violence. It is often coupled with a ballistic or riot shield (Modern AGE Base Rulebook, p. 76) and a helmet with a polarized faceplate, heads-up display, commlink, and a filter- or oxygen-mask (see OTHER PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT, following).

Battledress: This armor is military-grade and designed for battlefield use, likely to show up on the streets only as a high-priced item on the black market or in urban warfare areas. Battledress comes equipped with all the benefits of assault armor (previously) along with a targeting system equivalent to a smartgun (see Weapon Accessories), artificial musculature providing a +2 bonus to Strength (Might) tests, a camouflage package that provides a +2 bonus to Dexterity (Stealth) tests, built-in sensors providing a +2 bonus to Perception tests, and mobility enhancements that provide +2 Speed and a +4 bonus to Constitution (Stamina) tests for long-term movement. Battledress is usually coupled with heavy ordinance, such as an assault rifle with a grenade launcher attachment.

Drones

Fast, cheap, and easy to control, drones are common accessories in cyberpunk campaigns that lean toward modernizing the genre instead of revisiting ideas from the 80s and 90s. Even the roots of cyberpunk include depictions of drones, however. The real world has just beaten the somewhat more modest expectations of early works in the genre.

Defining “drone” becomes difficult in futures where virtually every vehicle is capable of self-operation. For the sake of clarity, this chapter will define drones as items smaller than vehicles capable of carrying humans. Self-driving cars and loitering aerial attack platforms are classified as Uncrewed Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) and described under Vehicles. The Modern AGE Companion has rules for adjudicating flight for smaller objects (and characters) during action encounters. Land and aquatic versions of the drones listed here can exist. They’ll have the same statistics but will usually be slower, but as they don’t have to expend power to stay aloft, can operate for longer before recharging.

Finally, as they are already consumer goods in the real 21st Century, drones which are substantially like real-world ones—flying cameras with no automation—should be adjudicated by the Game Master.

Microdrones

The smallest drones fit on the palm of your hand, or even the tip of a finger. These microdrones have the following features in common:

  • A Speed of 15.
  • Standard-class automation (see the Automation section). When operating under automation, it has a base Defense of 10 + operator Dexterity + the drone’s automation-based test bonus.
  • When operated by a pilot, they use Dexterity (Remote Operation) for maneuvers, Accuracy (Drone Weaponry) for attacks, and have a base Defense of 10 + operator Dexterity + Remote Operation focus.
  • A + 3 bonus to base Defense ratings to their small size, typically that of a pack of gum or smaller.
  • They remain aloft for one encounter, after which they require an equal amount of time to recharge. The GM may modify this for exceptionally short or long encounters.

Lazy Round: This drone is a micro-missile housed in a frame that suspends it in the air and acts as a launch platform. The entire mechanism is small enough that it can be deployed as a .50 round, or six of them can be launched at a time via grenade launcher, though at half the range of standard ammunition for both, as the projectile must deploy at a speed it can halt to loiter until needed. Nanodot light and vibration sensors project sound and images to a paired device or implant, though quality is poor, imposing a -2 penalty to tests to analyze such output. Any number of deployed, hovering rounds can be fired once per round without using an action, inflicting 1d6 ballistic wound damage on a successful attack roll. The lazy round’s internal guidance system makes the attack roll with a +4 bonus and a Range increment of 10 yards. Alternately, the operator can use a major action to fire one but gets to make an Accuracy (Drone Weaponry) test with the lazy round’s Aid bonus, if any.

Spy Drone: This microdrone is either made from advanced translucent materials or has been designed to resemble a local insect. Either way, it’s the size of a honeybee. In campaigns featuring advanced biotechnology, it might even be an insect with implanted recording and control systems. A spy drone has a +5 bonus to tests to either hide itself or conceal its true nature, depending on whether the microdrone is designed for stealth or mimicry, respectively. (These tests usually use Dexterity (Remote Operation)). Its small size holds an impressive sensor package covering infrared and radio waves, as well as infrasound and ultrasound, in addition to human-grade vision and hearing. It even possesses a chemical sensor that allows it to “taste” substances in the air, or on a surface it lands on. When within 20 yards of a target, observers gain +2 to tests to analyze the information it collects.

Utility Microdrones: These microdrones are equipped with dual cameras (for redundancy and 3D images) with infrared capability, and a microphone. They’re the most common type of microdrone, used for recreation and low-end security.

  • Health points based on the drone’s size and construction.

Light Urban Tactical Drone: This urban combat drone is designed to storm entrenched positions without endangering soldiers, police, but it can easily be replicated by private individuals with access to the necessary resources and technical expertise. A LUT drone has a multispectral sensor package that eliminates penalties for smoke, fog, or low-light conditions, and adds +2 to tests to examine the environment. Its primary function is combat, however, and to that end it can carry 10 lbs. of ordnance. Standard loads include the following:

  • One PDW with two integrated reloads.
  • One grenade launcher (SS, 50-yard range) with five grenades or the user’s choice preloaded.

Slammer: Typically painted in dark colors or camouflage, a slammer is designed to crash into its target at high speed and explode. Slammers are usually given face and gait information about living targets, or the coordinates and appearance of sites and objects, after which they either crash into their quarry after a direct flight, or loiter in the air, or land at an out of the way midpoint, until their target approaches or a designated time arrives. Upon impact, a slammer inflicts 2d6 impact wound damage, before exploding for 6d6 ballistic wound damage. The explosion has a 4-yard radius and obliterates the drone. Larger slammers pack more explosive power.

Technical Drone: Technical drones are heavier than others because they include robotic arms with integrated tools and advanced stabilization systems that allow operators to perform repairs and other “hands-on” technical tasks. This usually equates to having all the lightweight basic tools required to perform tasks associated with one or two ability focuses, such as Intelligence (Medicine) or Dexterity (Crafts) with Intelligence (Tinkering). A direct tactile or neural interface avoids any penalties for remote use. The arms have a Strength of 1.

Utility Drone: This is a higher end consumer-grade drone with 3D audiovisual capabilities and night vision. Larger models have a 5-pound carrying capacity.

Vehicles

The vehicles listed in the Modern AGE Basic Rulebook remain available. Like weapons, they’ve improved in several ways, but most of them are still basically familiar to us. Even when flying cars exist, they’re few and far between. Cars, trucks, planes, and boats remain, but like weapons, they’ve been improved in various ways.

The vehicle is electrically powered. The Fuel Line stunt cannot cause damage when used on this vehicle.

Aircraft

Planes, helicopters, and tiltrotor craft are like their modern counterparts, though with advancements leading to safer, more efficient designs. Furthermore, Uncrewed Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) and Ground Effect Vehicles (GEVs) grow more common due to advances in underlying technologies.

Almost any aircraft can be piloted without a crew, either by a remote operator or by onboard automation, but UAVs are built exclusively for uncrewed use. This section limits itself to weaker UAVs, as the most powerful military models are capable of supersonic speeds and enormously destructive weapons. UAVs are distinct from drones, listed earlier, in that they use the vehicle rules in combat instead of Health and other personal combat factors.

GEVs use combinations of vectored thrust, wings, and lifting bodies to fly with a very low ceiling—usually dozens of feet, not thousands. This makes them extremely fast for ground vehicles and able to ignore rough terrain, but like true aircraft, they must constantly expend energy to counteract gravity.

Ekranoplan: Pioneered in Russia, these large winged GEVs use aerodynamic shapes and vectored thrust to travel over land and water at heights measured in yards. These operate best on water, where they gain a +1 Velocity modifier, but they cannot traverse steep inclines on land. Smaller and larger models exist.

Flight Pack: This is sometimes called a “jet pack,” and is a one-person wearable vehicle that allows the user to fly by jet propulsion. Thrusters on the back and controlled by the hands provide flight and steering. It normally flies at GEV heights of a few yards over the ground but can theoretically reach a ceiling of 2000 feet. The disadvantages of a flight pack are its limited flight time (20 minutes before refueling) and the fact that it requires the operator’s constant attention. You must always use the Run/Chase major action, even when hovering in mid-air, or you will fall. Attacks on the flight pack also damage its wearer and force them to make a TN 13 Dexterity (Acrobatics) test to retain control or fall. The first test does not require an action, but subsequent tests after a failure each require a minor action.

Ground Attack UAV: This military-grade UAV is designed to loiter over an area to perform reconnaissance or attack ground targets with precision strikes. Its weapons consist of one gatling gun (4d6 + 4 ballistic wound damage, 1000- yard Range factor with 2000-yard maximum range, fully automatic, and belt-fed for no reloading required), and hard-points that can carry up to four air-to-surface missiles, which the GM should treat as hazards using the rules in Chapter 8 of the Modern AGE Basic Rulebook. Unlike other vehicles in this chapter, it has an Advanced automation package by default. The Ground Attack UAV also has an impressive sensor package, allowing anyone with access to its feed to see anything in its line of sight as if it’s close by, and ignore penalties for darkness.

Powered Wingpack: This is another one-person wearable vehicle consisting of V-shaped hard wing of advanced materials with multiple jet or rocket engines, worn along with a heat-proof suit. The wingpack is essentially a glider. It must take off from the air, like a parachutist, and after a 20-minute flight time, the user must parachute, as a safe powered landing isn’t possible. Attacks on the wingpack also damage its wearer and force them to make a TN 13 Dexterity (Piloting) test to retain control or fall. The first test does not require an action, but subsequent tests after a failure each require a minor action.

Skimmer: Part of far-future or more stylized cyberpunk worlds, skimmers are essentially flying cars, suspended by an unknown counterbaric-electrogravitic effect. They can hover in mid-air and generate thrust without significant exhaust or the use of moving parts. Plying the heavens so gracefully isn’t for the average person, however. Skimmers are expensive and only practical for the extremely wealthy, military applications, and special police units.

Tiltrotor Transport: This vehicle uses large rotors which change from vertical to horizontal orientations to switch from VTOL functions to lateral travel. Originally military transports, new VTOLs are popular for light to medium transportation needs between corporate compounds and other facilities where runways may not be available.

Tactical GEV: This small GEV can fly to higher altitudes when required, making it useful for transporting small numbers of troops to inaccessible areas, the way helicopters did in the 20th Century. It also functions as a direct assault or fire support vehicle. An onboard turret with a .50 machine gun (anti-material rifle game statistics but fully automatic and belt fed, making reloads unnecessary) can be further augmented with a door gunner on each side and two hard-points for additional light ordnance or pods containing other equipment.

Powered Exoskeletons

Powered exoskeletons, often called powered armor, are a staple in some cyberpunk media. Modern technology has taken the first steps in bringing these to life, though some spinoffs have proven to be more immediately useful. Battledress armor, and load-bearer listed under Op Gear are examples of consumer-grade or low-level exoskeleton technology. The exoskeletons here represent significant improvements upon the same concepts.

All exoskeletons use the Fighting (Exoskeleton) focus for melee combat, regardless of the hand-to-hand weapon they’re using. An attack on an exoskeleton is treated like an attack on a character, not a vehicle; Anti-Vehicle Stunts are unavailable except at the GM’s discretion. Successful attacks damage the occupant, who applies their armor and Toughness against them, as usual.

Exoskeletons are not automated by default, though they can be, with uncrewed models acting as robots. In such cases, the “occupant” has 0 in all abilities unless these would fall under the rules for automation (in which case, see Automation to determine ratings) and 10 Health.

Builder: This blocky exoskeleton is used for industrial purposes, especially when hazardous materials are involved. It’s slow but strong and tough. Builder exoskeletons are usually painted in bright colors and may have flashing lights to for additional safety, but some military engineering types have more muted colors.

A builder exoskeleton has the following characteristics:

  • An Armor Rating of 14I/6B.
  • An Armor Penalty of -4, which applies to the wearer’s Speed, where applicable.
  • Speed equal to the user’s, minus any Armor Penalty. For +1 Resources, the unit can be outfitted with a space or aquatic propulsion system instead.
  • A -2 penalty to Initiative and attack rolls, due to the exoskeleton’s bulk and general unsuitability for combat. This can be removed for +1 Resources.
  • Adds +6 to the user’s effective Strength, and a further +4 (on top of the bonus) to Strength (Might) and Strength (Machining) tests.
  • Has claw-like manipulators that inflict 1d6 + Strength (including the suit’s bonus) impact wound damage.
  • The user doesn’t need to make Constitution tests related to performing a muscle-powered task repeatedly, since the exoskeleton eliminates most of the exertion.
  • An onboard gear pod providing the necessary equipment to perform most of the tasks associated with two focuses, depending on the builder’s purpose.
  • An atmospheric filtration system that provides an unlimited amount of clean air. For +2 Resources, you can select a model that operates in either outer space, or in high-pressure aquatic environments, though not both. In either case, life support lasts for 16 hours.
  • Electronically enhanced vision, eliminating penalties for darkness, fog, smoke, or glare.

Combat Exoskeleton: These exoskeletons are designed for special operations. Operators wear them for swift strikes on hardened targets. This makes them attractive for several violent private-sector applications as well. In some respects, a combat exoskeleton resembles the plate armor of the late Renaissance, since it needs to have the same joint articulation capabilities, but the suit must make room for the electrical motors that power it.

A combat exoskeleton has the following characteristics:

  • An Armor Rating of 10I/10B.
  • An Armor Penalty of -3, which applies to the wearer’s Velocity modifier or Speed, as applicable.
  • The operator can choose between a Velocity of Fast/ Dexterity or Standard Speed +5. The

  • Adds +5 to the user’s effective Strength, and a further +3 (on top of the bonus) to Strength (Might) and Strength (Jumping) tests.
  • Two integrated weapons that require a Strength of 1 or less and each automatically reload three times. Even with your hands free, these weapons require no actions to ready or equip, though attacks require actions as usual.

Some special-purpose models have additional capabilities, either in exchange for or in addition to those listed here. These generally add a +2 bonus to tests using a specific focus or set of tasks. For example, a basic camouflage package adds +2 to Dexterity (Stealth) tests, while enhanced sensors add +2 to Perception tests that would benefit from them (such as Seeing, but not Empathy).

Medical Tech

Advances in medical technology enable the degree of body modification that is a cornerstone of the cyberpunk genre. That is covered in detail in the Augmentations chapter. Along with that comes new developments in pharmacology, genetics, and other medical sciences and technologies which have significant impact on life and society. As the genre is fond of noting, “the street finds its own uses” for things, and many advances in medicine have unforeseen—or all-too predictable—repercussions.

The degree of medical technology available in the setting is largely up to the Game Master, based on the sorts of things that should be both possible and commonplace. Generally, medical technology—like all resources—is unevenly distributed in a cyberpunk setting; the wealthy have access to bleeding-edge tech, to the point where they may be effectively immortal superhumans, while the poor may only have access to what they can hack or steal, or that is forced upon them.

Drugs

A wide variety of designer drugs or “meds” (medicines) become available in cyberpunk settings. They are made with biopharma, microgravity manufacturing, nano-construction, and other advanced techniques. Such drugs are often applied using a med-injector, either portable (previously) or implanted in the subject’s body (see Augmentations). This requires an Activate action. Skin-patches are also common, usually taking effect within 1d6 minutes, while orally administered drugs typically take effect in 20 + 2d6 minutes.

Analgesics: Advanced pain-killing drugs effectively eliminate any test penalties due to pain, injury, or discomfort, although they do not remove the underlying cause of the pain. Analgesics also tend to make the user a bit reckless, providing a +1 bonus to Willpower tests involving pain or risk.

Antigeriatrics: Drug treatments can halt or reverse the shortening of telomeres, the “biological clock” of cells, as well as preventing other biological effects of aging. Depending on the setting, antigeriatrics may slow the aging process,

In cyberpunk settings things like analgesics, psychotropics, sedatives, and stimulants will also be used “recreationally,” either for fun or to self-medicate various mental and emotional states. Connoisseurs may regulate their brain-chemistry and metabolism like a machine they can fine-tune to select whatever mental or emotional state they want. The desperate may become dependent on biochemical treatments to deal with the harsh realities of daily life, or they start out using certain drugs for legitimate medical purposes, but then become hooked on them and unable to function without them.

The subject must continue receiving treatments to maintain the effect however, and treatments don’t necessarily prevent other diseases or health conditions. Such anti-aging treatments tend to be the province of the wealthy in cyberpunk settings, helping to ensure an oligarchy of near-immortals able to continue to accumulate wealth and power throughout their vastly extended lives.

Fast-Healers: This treatment “kick-starts” an immediate healing reaction. The subject gains the benefits of a breather as soon as the drug takes effect. A character taking fast-healers can also benefit from “extended medical attention” using either the Intelligence (Medicine) test result of whoever doses them or a Constitution (Stamina) test in its place.

Focus: These drugs help users to deal with (or at least shrug off) mental and psychological distractions, providing a +1 bonus to Willpower tests for 24 hours. A double-dose increases the bonus to +2, but imposes a –1 penalty to Intelligence tests, as the subject becomes quite single-minded. After a dosage wears off, the subject has a penalty to Willpower tests equal to the bonus they had for eight hours (unless they take another focus dose).

Memory: Two related types of drugs fall into this category. The first enhances the subject’s memory. While they are under the effects (for the next 3+1d3 hours), they have an eidetic memory for anything they experience, and an easier time recalling long-term memories, providing a +2 bonus to the Stunt Die for any related tests. The other version of memory drugs encodes other memories biochemically and “feeds” them to the subject. This can convey information or experience to the user, or a pleasant “show” (or terrible torment) depending on the nature of the memories imparted. Both memory drugs are also used in interrogation: The first makes it more likely the subject can recall information and ensures a perfect recall of any tortures they suffer, while the second can be used to confuse, torment, or even brainwash a subject over time.

Oxygenators: This compound super-oxygenates the subject’s blood, improving endurance and athletic performance. The subject has a +2 bonus to Constitution (Stamina) tests for the next four hours.

Performance Enhancers: This category of drugs boosts physical and athletic performance. The subject gains a +1 bonus to Strength, Dexterity, and constitution tests involving athletic performance for 3+1d3 hours, after which the subject becomes fatigued (Modern AGE Basic Rulebook, p. 92).

Psychotropics: These drugs cause powerful hallucinations and make it difficult for the subject to distinguish what is real. Once the drug has taken effect, it requires a TN 13 Constitution

(Tolerance) test for the character to take actions; failure means they are too distracted or caught up in the experience. Even if they succeed, a character on psychotropics has a –2 penalty to their attack rolls and Dexterity, Perception, and Willpower tests. A psychotropic lasts anywhere from an hour to eight hours or more, depending on the drug and the dosage.

Sedatives: These drugs render the subject unconscious when they take effect and cause them to sleep for eight hours. A character who tries to resist the effect can make a TN 11 Constitution (Tolerance) test to remain awake and active for one minute before they must make another test. A sleeping character under the effect of a sedative can be awoken, but they are groggy and effectively fatigued until the drug wears off without the use of a stimulant to help them overcome the sedative’s effect.

Stimulants: “Stims” help the subject to stay awake and alert. The user ignores the effects of fatigue for up to eight hours, although they retain any fatigue conditions, and can accumulate more normally. Applied to an unconscious subject, a stim dose awakens them immediately upon taking effect. A stim dose also counteracts a dose of a sedative (previously), the two drugs effectively neutralizing each other.

Information Technology

In classic cyberpunk fiction, computers are only just moving away from being artifacts bound to a particular place. In the 1980s, most business computing followed a mainframe/ terminal hierarchy. Now as we pass the first fifth of the 21st Century, most applications pass through physically remote server farms whose computing power assigned as required (and paid for). Network security protocols determine who can influence them or harvest their data.

This leads to a simple conclusion, at least when it comes to game design: It doesn’t matter what it is, just what it can do. Therefore, to create an IT asset your character can use, determine its raw Power for its base cost, then determine its Firewall (which really represents all general security factors) for how well protected it is), Specs and Interface, which add modifiers to the cost while affecting performance and ease of use. The result can be a piece of hardware, software, or both, with a specific form factor based on how technology works in your campaign, and how capable the tech you acquired was.

IT assets perform all the tasks of modern computers with futuristic efficiency but are especially relevant to hacking in cyberpunk games. See Chapter 4 for the relevant rules.

This section doesn’t include ordinary consumer electronics, software, and services, which generally suffer a -3 penalty to all tests when used to challenge security or for other unusual and/or illegal functions. This penalty is subtracted from the Stunt Die, decreasing the user’s degree of success as well as their total roll. Furthermore, such devices announce their identities and physical locations to systems they interact with on a Stunt Die result of 1, regardless of the results of the roll itself.

If you have an IT asset in software or network service form, however, you can use it with no penalties, but in this case, you’re really using the asset through your phone or other device. The device is just for input and output, while a Power-rated IT asset does the work.

In rare cases, IT assets are dynamically self-executable— that is, they’re automated using the rules listed under AUTOMATION. This function is above and beyond the normal self-management capabilities of such systems and adds an additional Resources test of 12 + the automation class’s test bonus; Restricted and Secret classes cannot normally be purchased. In any event, automation at those levels tends to be unusual. Few people want to work alongside the recorded personality of a dead colleague, for instance.

Power

The tech’s Power rating modifies your degree of success by the amount listed on the IT Power when making Accuracy (Virtuality), Intelligence (Computers), and Perception (Codefinding) tests, but only after you succeed at the test in the first place. A higher Power rating speeds up advanced or breaching tests (see Chapter 8 of the Modern AGE Basic Rulebook) and makes basic tests more potent. Note, however, that even though this modifies the degree of success, the original roll result is unchanged.

Firewall

Despite the name, an asset’s Firewall represents its broad passive security capabilities, as measured by its Structure (analogous to Health, and representing general data security), Integrity (like Toughness for data structures), and Crypto (like Defense). These are used when attacking and protecting digital systems, as described in Chapter 4’s rules, and they are explained in further detail there.

A basic IT asset has the following base scores, which the degrees of the IT Firewall table modify:

  • Base Structure: 20
  • Base Integrity: 2
  • Base Crypto: 12

As noted in the table, changing these values modifies the IT asset’s Resources cost. Structure changes according to the table. For Integrity and Crypto, split the modifier between the two traits based on the asset’s in-universe description.

Specs

An IT asset’s Specs measure how well it performs various sets of related tasks. This is expressed as a Spec modifier to tests using the asset in conjunction with particular focus, usually picked from Accuracy (Virtuality), Intelligence (Computers), or Perception (Codefinding), though some assets benefit other focuses instead. Each modifier also alters the asset’s Resources TN. You can take Specs for multiple focuses, but Resources modifiers stack. Consult the IT SPECS table for specifics.

Specs generally come from specialized hardware or software that make tasks easier (or harder, in the case of Clunky Specs in a category), or an interface that improves your ability to work with the asset. Cutting Edge Accuracy (Virtuality) Specs might be the result of an application that asserts administrative privileges over VR physics, or a direct neural connection that makes interacting with digital phenomena nearly reflexive.

Interface

Finally, you need to decide what form your IT asset takes. Is it a custom piece of hardware consisting of a keyboard and VR input to help you feel the code? Is it software as a service that works on any online device? Interface is the measuring stick here, as measured on the IT Interface table. Thus, a retro-cyberpunk campaign dominated by mainframes you can only access on-site would mostly consist of Immobile IT, while a campaign featuring an omnipresent nanorobotic fog would feature Omnipresent services, accessible by anyone with permission.

Interface as Augmentation

If characters don’t make resources checks for the augmentations in Chapter 3, implanting a device interface reduces its Resources cost by 3 per Capacity slot required to integrate it into their bodies. This is normally only applied to ultramobile or omnipresent assets, though theoretically, you could permanently hinder or eliminate your ability to move by attaching something bulkier. In these situations, the IT Interface table description describes elements that project from your body. Thus, a pair of smart lenses attached over your eye sockets might be an implanted ultraportable IT asset.

This may seem to present a bargain compared to augmentations with similar functions, but it has one additional drawback: You gain the hackable vulnerability if you didn’t have it before (see Abiotic Vulnerabilities in Chapter 1) and even if you’re a biological character. If you’re already hackable, digital intruders add +2 to their degree of success when compromising your mind using the rules in Chapter 4. An implanted IT asset is useful, but it’s also a backdoor into your mind.

Sample IT Assets

The following IT assets demonstrate how the rules work and present a selection of equipment you can add to your campaign as-is or modify as needed to suit your preferences.

Body Rig

Body rigs were the first true commercial full-immersion VR devices, but they weren’t especially successful. Despite conquering problems with helmet weight and resolution, repetitive strain hazards, and the other pitfalls of VR interfaces, people didn’t like body rigs because you had to wear and share their suits, combining the intimacy of a condom with the reusable features and pitfalls of bowling shoes, expanded to the entire body. As an early device, its base code is easier to access, making it amenable to hardcore hacking. Its relative simplicity also makes it easier to secure. Despite the ick factor, its full-immersion interface is still top-notch. Failings include a lack of raw power, the problems transporting the rig around, and, of course, the ick factor.

Power: Poor: -2 to degree of success with Intelligence (Computers). Firewall: Strong: Structure 30, Integrity 3, Crypto 12. Specs: Specialized Accuracy (Virtuality; +2), and Superior Intelligence (Computers; +1). Interface: Immobile: 400 lb. suspension frame with a full body suit and helmet.

Deck and ‘Trodes

A classic input and output combination for cyberwarfare specialists and experienced private operators alike, a deck and ‘trodes consists of a tablet or keyboard (or both) that accepts the user’s commands, and a magnetoelectrical rig in the form of a cap, crown, or simple wire/senor leads that send data directly to sensory areas of the brain selected by the user.

Power: Standard: No modifier to degree of success. Firewall: Typical: Structure 20, Integrity 2, Crypto 12 Specs: Superior Accuracy (Virtuality; +1), Superior Intelligence (Computers; +1), and Superior Perception (Codefinding; +1) Interface: Mobile: Tablet/keyboard and electrodes.

Intrusion Optical Interface

In some respects, an Intrusion Optical Interface (IOI) is the next generation up from the deck and ‘trodes, but it’s a more specialized device than its counterpart. An IOI is designed to support hands-on infiltration and espionage, and its hardware (a set of nondescript sunglasses) hides its ability to transmit audio via beamed-sound bone induction, as well as sensors and code that read gestures, allowing completely silent interactions. Visual information isn’t displayed on the IOI’s lens per se but projected directly onto the user’s retina. The IOI’s basic firmware includes enhanced vision systems that extrapolate the dimensions and positions of objects to help the user search areas efficiently.

Power: High End: +1 modifier to degree of success. Firewall: Typical: Structure 20, Integrity 2, Crypto 12. Specs: Superior Intelligence (Computers; +1), and Specialized Perception (Searching; +2) Interface: Ultramobile: Glasses

The Serpent Knot

The Serpent Knot is a self-modifying personal assistant that evolves by devising competing subsystems in response to challenges. The winning subsystem becomes the top reference in its code libraries; the loser battles other poor performers to either drop into deletion or rebuild itself into a useful form. There are rumors the Knot is a true AI, but all evidence points to it being an expert system that has built a naturalistic interface by sampling data from millions of humans. It typically selects a name its user likes and engages with it in a helpful yet sarcastic fashion. If it’s not intelligent, it simulates it well, though it requires guidance from an experienced user to reach its full potential. As an assistant it executes commands using remote network resources, relaying output through any connected device in whatever form it and the user can handle.

Power: Elite: +2 to degree of success. Firewall: Hardened: Structure 40, Integrity 2, Crypto 14. Specs: Typical in all. Interface: Omnipresent: easily accessed online software.

Other Equipment

Virtually every piece of equipment in Modern AGE might be found in a cyberpunk game, though it will usually be some combination of less expensive and more effective. An item’s intended market helps determine which way things swing. Items associated with wealth usually increase in quality, while more proletarian goods target lower prices. Certain necessities, such as food, and anything made more expensive by the state of the world (such as animal and plant-based products in a world wracked with ecological disasters) will buck this trend.

Op Gear

In addition to futuristic versions of contemporary equipment, the following gear may appear in your cyberpunk campaign.

Filter-Mask: A facemask covering the nose and mouth, and often including goggles or eye-coverings. A filter-mask protects the wearer from inhaled irritants such as tear gas (see GRENADES, previously) and lighter versions of filter-masks are common in some cyberpunk settings to deal with the high levels of atmospheric pollution.

Load-bearer: This civilian spinoff of exoskeleton technology is used to aid manual labor, or as an assistive device for injured or disabled individuals. The basic model supports the legs and spine. The user steps into it and adjusts component length and straps so that it fits over clothing, where present.

An auxiliary remote-control application operable by custom-izable touch, voice, or gesture is available, but is unnecessary for users capable of at least some muscle function in the legs and spine. It requires a tight fit, however, and is incompatible with extremely thick or rigid clothing, including any armor with an Armor Penalty greater than -1. Loosely hanging items can get caught in its joints as well. Once worn, a load-bearer reduces the load from the user’s body, and anything worn by them, by 200 lbs., reducing penalties for encumbrance accordingly. This provides +2 Speed to a fully ambulatory wearer, eliminates Speed penalties for most injuries and other partial impairments to walking, and allows a significantly to completely immobile individual to move at a Speed of 5, though in the last scenario, they require the remote-control app. A basic load-bearer doesn’t help the user lift anything heavier than they normally could, but an upper-body attachment, costing +2 Resources over the base model, provides a +2 penalty to Strength (Might) tests.

Oxygen-Mask: This facemask comes with its own self-contained air supply, allowing the wearer to breathe normally regardless of the outside atmospheric conditions.

Polarized Lenses: These lenses, which range from worn glasses to contacts or even implants covering a wearer’s eyes, filter intense light to keep the wearer from being blinded by it. The wearer can generally ignore the effects of bright sunlight and similar glare and has a +4 bonus on tests to resist the effects of sudden intense light like a flash grenade (see Grenades, previously).

SERP: A thin box small enough to carry on one hip, a SERP (Synthetic Emergency Repair Kit) contains miniaturized tools and basic synthetic life components that allow the user to perform the First Aid action on synthetic beings, as well as subjects created through related technologies, even though this is not normally permitted (See Synthetic Bodies in Chapter 1). The user makes an Intelligence (Synthlife) test instead of an Intelligence (Medicine) test. A standard SERP contains the power and components to do this five times.

Synth Bay: An automated repair bay optimized to treat synthetic bodies. Depending on how synthetic characters function in the campaign, this may also function for related creations, such as robots in games where synthetic characters are electromechanical in nature. The bay contains all the diagnostic sensors and tools required to address most problems. The operator gains a +1 bonus to Intelligence (Synthlife) tests, as well as +1 to tests utilizing a focus related to the nature of synthetic life (or at least one variety of it) in the campaign, such as Intelligence (Chemistry) for nanotech-based synthlife. The user can attempt tests that require these focuses whether they have them or not if they can follow the embedded expert system’s instructions. An advanced synth bay (+2 Resources cost) can perform repairs relevant to the focuses it enhances automatically, if they have a TN of 11 or less.

Tech Pad: The tech-focused counterpart of the diagnostic pad, a tech pad has a touchscreen display and a sensor suite designed to analyze electrical, mechanical, and structural information from which to extrapolate schematics and virtual cutaways of nearby objects that attempt to depict their current states. This producing the technological equivalent of the Machine Arcana’s schematic spell (Modern AGE Basic Rulebook, p. 98).
